notes: Those sentences, precisely. Of 1,000,000 programs of sixty-four random bytes, 4,064 were refused by Ethereum before they existed (their first byte was 0xEF; the protocol forbids it) — 0.4%, against a predicted 1 in 256. Of the 995,936 installed, 78.4% halted on their very first instruction. The longest life was 12 instructions. Across 4,979,680 calls, 0.8% ended cleanly; 54.1% on a byte that is not an instruction; 44.9% reaching for an operand that was not there.

“Listened”: 107 programs behaved differently depending on what they were called with — the data, or the money. “Remembered”: 5 wrote to persistent storage and then halted cleanly, so the write survived. “Attempted reproduction”: 17 executed CREATE or CREATE2; none produced a child. Either the creation itself failed — the value it tried to send was a random constant larger than any balance — or the parent halted exceptionally moments later and undid it. No child program ever existed on the chain. 25 returned data. 251 ran out of gas — every one by asking a single instruction for more memory than any gas can buy; none by looping.

Lifespan is geometric: about 22% of programs survive each instruction, and the next, and the next. Of 256 possible byte values, 55 are instructions that need no operands; a random first byte is one of them with probability 0.215. Everything else follows from that.

Method: random bytes placed by CREATE behind a fixed eleven-byte loader on a local chain, code verified byte for byte, then called five ways under a 1,000,000-gas ceiling with every opcode traced. Nothing was filtered, weighted or retried. The harness and the write-ups are in the repository.
